blocks.text: I can use a light microscope to observe and produce scientific drawings of cells.
Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: A type of microscope that uses visible light and a system of lenses to generate magnified images of small objects.
A piece of glass or other transparent material with curved sides, used in a microscope to magnify objects.
Making small objects appear larger in order to see more detail.
A point where light rays converge to form an image.

blocks.text: Use the word {magnification}, not “zoom in”. And say “{focus} the image” rather than “make the image clearer”.
Tap each part to see its job.

items.def: The part you look down when you view your specimen.
There are usually three objective lenses. You change them to change the magnification of the image.
The slide with the specimen goes on the stage, under the clips. The stage can move up and down to get closer to or further from the objective lenses.
At the bottom of the microscope. The light must shine directly through the specimen so that you can view it.
The initial focusing wheel. It moves the stage towards or further away from the objective lens.
Gives a much more precise image, so you can focus much more clearly.

blocks.text: Here are the first three steps of the method for using a light microscope.

items: **Turn the objective lens to the lowest magnification.**
**Place the slide on the stage under the clips.**
**Turn on the light source.**

blocks.text: Make sure the specimen is over the little hole in the stage, so that the light can shine through it.
Careful! Lamps can get very hot.

items: **Looking from the side**, turn the coarse focus wheel to move the stage up so it is close to the objective lens.
**Looking into the eyepiece lens**, turn the coarse focus wheel to bring your specimen into focus.
Turn the **fine focus wheel** to sharpen the focus of the image.
To increase the magnification, change to a **higher power objective lens**.

blocks.label: Why look from the side when moving the stage up?
blocks.text: So you can see when to stop moving the stage upwards, so that it does not smash into the objective lens.

blocks.q: Match each part of the microscope to its job.

pairs.b: brings the specimen roughly into focus

items.q: What is the very first step?
options: Turn the objective lens to the lowest magnification
Change to the highest power objective lens
On the stage, under the clips

items.q: Which wheel do you turn first to bring the specimen into focus?
How do you increase the magnification?
options: Change to a higher power objective lens

options: To see when to stop so the stage does not smash into the objective lens

blocks.text: A light microscope can be used to observe animal and plant cells. Images like these may be similar to what you see:
In each image you can see lots of cells of the same type. That is a {tissue}. Look carefully and try to spot one **single cell**.
You can record what you see in a **labelled scientific line drawing** of cells. It does not look exactly the same as the original image. It is a clear and simple representation.
The rules for a scientific line drawing of cells:

items: select a **few** cells
use **continuous** lines (no sketching)
make the lines **smooth and joined up**
**no shading** apart from stippling
draw it a **large size**
add **clear labels**, including the magnification (for example x400)

blocks.label: What is stippling?
blocks.text: Stippling means using dots with your pencil.

blocks.q: Should a scientific line drawing of cells have this?

blocks.text: Magnification is a measure of how many times an object has been enlarged. The **image size** is the size of the picture or drawing. The **real size** is the actual size of the cell.
The real size is much smaller than the image size, so always check that your image size is the bigger one.
The image size and the real size must be in the **same unit** before you divide. How many are there in one metre?

items: To go to the next smaller unit (m to mm, mm to µm, µm to nm), **multiply by 1000**.
To go back to the next bigger unit, **divide by 1000**.
Centimetres to millimetres: multiply by 10.

blocks.text: A red blood cell has a diameter of 8 µm. In an image it measures 5.6 mm. Calculate the magnification.

items: Same units first: 5.6 mm × 1000 = 5600 µm.
magnification = image ÷ real = 5600 ÷ 8.
5600 ÷ 8 = 700, so the magnification is x700.

blocks.label: Check it
blocks.text: The image size (5600 µm) is bigger than the real size (8 µm), as it should be.
The image of a mitochondrion measures 3.0 mm and is magnified x5000. Calculate its real size, in micrometres.

items: real size = image ÷ magnification.
Convert to micrometres: 0.0006 × 1000 = 0.6 µm.

items.q: A cell is 20 µm long. In an image it measures 4 mm. What is the magnification?
A plant cell is 50 µm across. In an image it measures 12 mm. What is the magnification?
In an image a structure measures 6 mm and the magnification is x300. What is its real size?
A structure is 25 µm long. The magnification is x400. How long is it in the image?

items: A light microscope can be used to observe animal and plant cells.
Follow the method: lowest magnification first, slide on the stage, light on, coarse focus wheel, then fine focus wheel; change to a higher power objective lens to increase the magnification.
Observations can be recorded in a labelled scientific line drawing.
The magnification and real size of structures can be calculated: magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Light microscopy: observing and drawing cells
worksheet.instructions: Answer each question with a word or a number. For the calculations, convert to the same units first and give the answer in the unit asked for.

questions.prompt: Which part of a light microscope do you look down to view the specimen?
questions.explanation: The eyepiece lens is the part you look down.

questions.prompt: You change this part of the microscope to change the magnification. Name it (two words).
questions.explanation: Changing to a higher power objective lens increases the magnification.

questions.prompt: Which wheel do you turn first to bring the specimen into focus?
questions.explanation: The coarse focus wheel is the initial focusing wheel; the fine focus wheel is used afterwards to sharpen the focus.

questions.prompt: Which word should you use instead of “zoom in”?
questions.explanation: Magnification means making small objects appear larger in order to see more detail.

questions.prompt: How many micrometres (µm) are there in 1 millimetre (mm)? Write a number.
Convert 3 mm to micrometres (µm). Write a number.
questions.explanation: mm to µm: multiply by 1000, so 3 × 1000 = 3000.

questions.prompt: Calculate the magnification of a mitochondrion with a length of 0.8 µm in an image measuring 14 mm. Give the number only.
Calculate the magnification of a flea’s leg with a length of 1.2 mm in an image measuring 15 cm. Give the number only.
Calculate the real size of a pollen grain given an image size of 30 mm and a magnification of 400x. Give your answer in mm.
Calculate the real size of a bacterium with an image size of 0.25 mm and a magnification of 2000x. Give your answer in µm.
Calculate the image size of a human hair strand with a real size of 20 µm and a magnification of 500x. Give your answer in mm.
questions.explanation: image size = 20 × 500 = 10 000 µm, which is 10 mm.
